summary: This Level 3 unit is about putting fabricated parts together into accurate, safe assemblies such as frames, stands, gates, trusses and platforms. You will plan an assembly and its sub-assemblies, set out and check size, square, level and flatness, build and prove simple jigs, fit and tack joints, control distortion, and join parts by welding, bolting and riveting. You will also lift and install assemblies safely, inspect and record the work, hand it over, and lead a small team.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers the **assembly** of fabricated components: taking parts that have been cut, drilled and formed, and putting them together, to the drawing, into a finished item that is the right size, square, safe and ready to hand over.

Most of what a Jamaican fabrication shop sells is an assembly: gates and grilles, water-tank stands, stair and handrail frames, roof trusses, racks, platforms, trailer frames and machine guards. A part can be cut perfectly and still end up in a frame that is out of square, twisted or too big for its opening. Assembly is where accuracy is won or lost.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and fabricators who plan the order of work, set the checks, lead a small team and sign off the result.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at Level 3
rows: Read the drawings and parts list, split the job into sub-assemblies, set the order of work, the hold points, the people and the lifts.
Use datums, tolerances, section sizes and weld symbols; work out lengths, totals and clearances.
Set out full size, and check size, square, flatness, level and plumb with the right tools; allow for heat and tool errors.
Build and prove simple jigs with stops and clamps; use strongbacks, wedges and magnets correctly.
Check fit-up before welding; tack to the procedure; choose pre-set, sequence and restraint to keep the job in shape.
Choose bolt grade, holes, washers, tightening order and torque; choose and set rivets; set anchors.
Plan lifts, estimate weights, use lifting gear safely, and install items such as gates plumb and level.
Measure and record actual sizes, deal with non-conformances, and put together a handover pack.
Brief, give roles, supervise at hold points, coach, and keep the area safe.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, drawings, setting out, jigs, fit-up, distortion, fastening, lifting, inspection and supervision.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as datum, gusset, camber, base plate, NDT) and calculations; and longer answers that explain a plan, a method or a check.

**Group practical tasks**: building a jig and two identical frames with a fit-up hold point and a dimensional report; and assembling a bolted and welded stand from sub-assemblies with a torque record and a handover pack.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to the theory papers. Practise Pythagoras, totals from a parts list, clearances and tolerance sums until they are quick and sure.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: The whole item, how the parts go together, overall sizes, weld symbols and fixings
Each part: its size, holes, bevels and bends
Every part's mark number, description, size, material and quantity
Drawing number and **revision**, scale, units, general tolerances, the material and finish
The welding procedure, bolt grades, torques, coating, inspection and any special checks

blocks.note: Always work from the **latest revision** of a drawing. Building to an old one is one of the commonest causes of costly rework.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Large items are built from smaller **sub-assemblies**: a gate from its leaves and frame, a tank stand from its side frames and top frame, a platform from its deck and legs.

ul: Faults are easier to find and fix on a small part than on the finished item.
Sub-assemblies can be built at the same time by different people.
They are easier to lift, turn over, paint or galvanise, and carry to site.
Items that are bolted together on site travel as sub-assemblies.
Plan the order so that **every joint can be reached** for welding, grinding and bolting. Some joints cannot be reached once other parts are fitted, so they are welded first.
Build and check each sub-assembly before it is joined to others.
Weld inside corners and hidden faces before the item is closed in.
Plan where the item will be turned over, and how.
Put **hold points** in the plan: stages where work stops until a check is made and signed.

blocks.p: Check parts coming from the cutting, drilling and forming bays against the parts list **before** assembly starts: size, number, material, hole positions, bevels and bends. Mark each part with its mark number. A wrong part found now costs minutes; found after welding, it costs hours.

flow: Read the drawings, parts list and specification; note the tolerances and special checks
Check every part against the list and mark it
Split the job into sub-assemblies and set the order of work, leaving access for every joint
Decide how each part will be located and held: table, jig, stops, clamps
Plan the welding order to control distortion
Set the hold points and the checks at each one
Plan the lifts, the people and their roles, the tools and consumables
Write it down, brief the team, and record the checks as the job goes

blocks.h: Jobs that are bolted together on site

ul: Check every part, bolt, nut, washer, anchor and tool against the list before the load leaves the shop. A missing washer on a hillside site can stop the job for a day.
Where you can, **trial assemble** the item in the shop: bolt it up, check it, then **match-mark** the joints (paint or stamped marks) so each part goes back in the same place on site.
Pack small fixings in labelled bags or boxes, by joint.
Protect coated surfaces for the journey.

head: Section
How the size is written (example)
Typical uses
rows: Square or rectangular hollow section (SHS, RHS, box section)

head: Part
What it is
rows: A plate welded to the bottom of a column or leg, with holes for the holding-down bolts
A triangular plate welded into a corner to stiffen it
A small plate or piece of angle used to connect one member to another
A plate welded to a member to stop it buckling or bending

blocks.p: A **datum** is the point, line or edge from which measurements are taken. Good drawings give the main sizes from a datum, and you mark out from the same datum. If you measure each mark from the last one instead, every small error is added to the next.

No part is made to an exact size, so the drawing gives a **tolerance**: how far the size may vary. 1 200 ± 2 mm means anything from 1 198 mm to 1 202 mm is accepted. Frames also have a tolerance on squareness, often given as the largest allowed difference between the two diagonals.

**Tolerances add up.** When parts are fitted end to end, the worst possible error is the sum of their tolerances. Five parts at ±1 mm each could be up to ±5 mm out in total. So the plan sets out long runs from a datum, and allows adjustment where parts meet.

head: Problem
How to work it out
Example
rows: Add every length on the parts list
Joints × bolts per joint × items per bolt
2 450 mm opening − 2 410 mm gate = 40 mm in total

blocks.p: Assembly drawings show welds with symbols. In the AWS system a symbol has an **arrow** pointing at the joint and a horizontal **reference line**.

head: Feature
Meaning
rows: Weld on the **arrow side** of the joint (the side the arrow touches)
Weld on the **other side** of the joint
Fillet weld; the size (leg) is written to its left
Two numbers to the right, such as 50-150
Intermittent weld: 50 mm long welds at 150 mm centres (pitch)
Small **flag** where the arrow meets the reference line
Site (field) weld: made on site, not in the shop
Small **circle** where the arrow meets the reference line
Tail (a V at the end of the line)
A note: the process, the procedure or another reference

blocks.note: Drawings to the ISO system show arrow side and other side differently (with a dashed line). Check which system the drawing uses before you read it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Tool
Used for
Points to watch
rows: Check it against a known length before a big job: a bent or worn hook makes every reading wrong
The hook slides by its own thickness, so pushed and hooked readings both come out right; do not fix it tight
Read square on, not at an angle
Check them now and then against a known square
Store it flat or hanging so it does not bend
Check it by reversing it end for end on the same surface
Plumb, straight lines, and twist checks
Projects a level (or plumb) line or plane across a site to set and check heights
Set up on firm ground; follow the maker's safety rules for the beam
Root gaps, bevel angles, mismatch and weld sizes
Use the right gauge for the joint

blocks.p: A large frame is often set out **full size** on a flat, level setting-out table or floor. Chalk lines and stops are fixed from a **datum corner**, so each part can be placed to the lines and checked before it is tacked. The same layout then serves every frame of that type.

ul: A rectangle is square when its **two diagonals are equal**. Measure both, corner to corner, at the same points on each corner.
The **3-4-5 rule**: mark 3 units along one side and 4 along the other; when the line between the marks is 5 units, the corner is square. Multiples (600-800-1 000 mm) are more accurate on big frames.
**Pythagoras**: the long side of a right-angled triangle squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides (c² = a² + b²). Use it for diagonals, rafters and braces.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A truss has a span of 6 000 mm and a rise of 1 250 mm at the centre. Each rafter runs from a corner to the centre: half the span (3 000 mm) across and 1 250 mm up. Rafter = √(3 000² + 1 250²) = √(9 000 000 + 1 562 500) = √10 562 500 = **3 250 mm** (centre line).

A frame can be square and still **twisted** ("in wind"): one corner lifts off a flat table. Stretch two strings across the diagonals: if they just touch where they cross, the frame is flat. If one passes clear of the other, or pushes it aside, the frame is twisted. Straight edges across the frame and feeler gauges under its corners also show twist and bow.

ul: **Level** means horizontal; **plumb** means truly vertical.
Check posts and legs for plumb on **two faces** at right angles.
On site, a laser level or a water level sets matching heights across a long distance.

blocks.p: Steel grows as it warms: about **0.012 mm per metre for every 1 °C**. A frame in the afternoon sun can be far hotter than the air. A 6 m member that warms by 25 °C grows 6 × 0.012 × 25 = **1.8 mm**. For close tolerances, measure the job and the tape at the same temperature, preferably in the shade or in the cool of the morning, and note the time of a check.

blocks.note: A black steel frame in a yard under the midday Jamaican sun can get hot enough to burn your hand. Expect readings to differ from the morning ones, and do not "correct" a frame that is only warm.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **jig** (or fixture) holds parts in exactly the right place while they are fitted and welded, so that every item made in it is the same. For a run of identical frames, a jig saves marking out each one and makes every frame fit its opening.

ul: **Built on a flat, level base**, usually the setting-out table.
**Stops** (blocks, angle pieces or pins) fixed from a datum locate each part. A part is pushed against its stops, so it sits in the same place every time.
**Clamps** hold the part against its stops, placed where they do not block the welds and do not get in the welder's way.
**Foolproof**: a part can only go in one way.
**Easy to unload**: as the welds cool the frame shrinks, so stops **inside** a frame get gripped tight. Put stops on the outside, or use removable pins inside.
**Allows for shrinkage**: if the first frame comes out small, set the stops out by that amount and prove the jig again.
**Checked at intervals**: stops can be knocked or work loose.

flow: Mark the outline full size from the drawing, starting from a datum corner
Fix the stops at the corners and at each rail
Add clamps, clear of the joints
Make the first item (the "first-off") and measure it fully after welding and release
Adjust the stops for any shrinkage and prove the jig again
Record the jig check; recheck it at set intervals and whenever readings start to drift

head: Tool
Use
Watch out for
rows: Holding parts to stops or to each other
Spatter on the screw; fingers trapped as parts close up
Fast, repeated clamping on a jig
Set the pressure so thin parts are not bent
Holding parts at 90° or 45° while tacking
They can pull the arc off line (arc blow), and they weaken when hot: move them before welding near them
Closing gaps and pushing edges level
Do not force a bad fit together: find out why it does not fit
A stiff bar fixed across a plate joint, with wedges, to hold the edges level for welding
Remove it after welding, grind off its tacks and check the plate
Remove spacers before they are welded in, unless the procedure says otherwise

blocks.p: A part clamped hard and welded holds stresses inside it. When the clamps come off, it may **spring** a little out of line. Leave work clamped until it has **cooled**: hot steel is still shrinking and moving. If a part always springs the same way, allow for it in the jig.

blocks.note: Clamps, magnets and closing parts trap fingers. Keep your hands clear as parts come together, and never put your fingers between a part and a stop.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **fit-up** check is made after parts are tacked and **before full welding**: a fault found now is cheap to fix. It is usually a hold point, signed off before welding starts.

ul: The right parts, in the right place and the right way round.
Main sizes with a tape; square by the diagonals; flat by strings or straight edges.
At each joint: root gap, root face and bevel angle with gauges; edges level, with no step (**mismatch**).
Joint faces clean of rust, paint, oil and slag.
Tacks sound, the right size, not cracked.
Every joint can be reached by the welder.

head: Fit-up fault
Right action
Wrong action
rows: Root gap too wide in one place
Break the tacks and re-fit to the right gap
Bridge the gap with a piece of rod, or fill it with many passes
Bring them level with clamps or a strongback before welding
Weld it as it is and grind the high side
Frame out of square while tacked
Break the corner tacks, pull it square with a clamp across the long diagonal, re-tack and re-check
Weld it and hope the welds pull it back

ul: Tacks **become part of the final weld**, so they are made with the same care and to the same procedure (including preheat, if the procedure asks for it).
Make them big enough not to crack, but small enough to be melted in.
On joints that will be welded over, grind the ends of each tack to a **taper**, so the final weld fuses smoothly into it.
Tack in a balanced order, for example opposite corners in turn.

blocks.p: The weld and the steel beside it expand when hot and shrink as they cool. The cold steel around holds them back, so the shrinking pulls the parts out of shape.

head: Kind of distortion
What happens
rows: The member gets shorter along the weld
Parts are pulled closer together across the weld
The parts close up, like a book closing, about the weld
A long member bends along its length, because welds are on one side
A frame or beam winds out of flat

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Gaps right and welds no bigger than the drawing asks: less weld metal means less shrinkage
Where the drawing allows, less heat and less weld metal go in
Opposite sides or corners welded in turn so the pulls cancel
Weld from the centre outwards; use back-step or skip welding on long joints
Jigs, clamps and strongbacks hold the work; leave it held until cool
Set a part slightly the other way (for example an upright leaning away from a one-sided weld) so shrinkage pulls it true; find the amount by a trial
Build a slight upward curve into a beam on purpose so it is straight when it carries its load

blocks.note: If distortion still happens, small errors may be corrected by pulling with clamps or by **flame straightening**, only as the supervisor directs. Some joints must be cut and re-welded.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A metric bolt is described by its thread size and length: **M12 × 50** is 12 mm thread, 50 mm long. The head is marked with its **property class** (strength grade).

head: Property class
Minimum tensile strength
Yield (where it starts to stretch for good)
Matching nut class

blocks.p: The first number × 100 gives the tensile strength in MPa; the second number × 10 gives the yield as a percentage of it. The **nut must match** the bolt grade: a weaker nut can strip its thread before the bolt is tight.

ul: Drill holes to the size on the drawing, usually a little bigger than the bolt (often 1–2 mm) so it fits without forcing. Holes that are too big let the joint slip.
Clamp mating parts together and **drill them as a pair** so the holes line up exactly. Centre punch, then drill a pilot hole on larger sizes.
**Slotted holes** give a little adjustment to line a part up on site.

Never enlarge or line up a hole with a cutting torch, and never hammer a drift through to force holes into line. If holes do not line up, stop and find out why; any reaming or re-drilling needs approval.
**Washers** spread the load and protect the surface; use hardened or tapered washers where the specification asks.
At least one full thread should show past the nut (or as the specification says).

flow: Fit all bolts in the joint, with washers, finger-tight
Snug them up so the parts are pulled into full contact
Tighten in a criss-cross order, working from the centre of the joint outwards
Final tightening with a torque wrench to the figure the specification or maker gives (in newton metres, N m)
Paint-mark each nut and bolt end as it is done, and record the torque

blocks.p: A torque figure is given for a thread condition. **Oil, wax or grease cuts friction**, so the same torque pulls the bolt much tighter and can stretch or snap it. Use the figure for dry or for lubricated threads, as the bolts are. **Thread locker** (a liquid that sets) or lock nuts stop nuts working loose where there is vibration.

blocks.note: Treat the torque wrench as a measuring tool: keep it calibrated, never use it to undo bolts, and (for click types) wind it back to its lowest setting after use.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Blind rivets** (pop rivets) are set from one side: useful on sheet, hollow sections and coated parts.
Choose the length from the maker's **grip range**: the total thickness of the parts must fall within it. Drill the hole size the maker gives.
Keep rivets back from the edge (a common rule is at least **2 rivet diameters**) and apart (often at least 3 diameters), or as the drawing says.
Use rivets of the **same metal** as the parts. Two different metals touching in wet or salty air corrode (galvanic corrosion).
A loose or badly set rivet is drilled out and replaced, never hammered tighter.
**Cast-in** holding-down bolts are set in the concrete with a template that holds them at the exact spacing and height.
**Drilled anchors** (expansion or chemical) are set exactly as the maker says: hole size and depth, cleaning the hole, and curing time.
Do not load a stand or tighten anchors until the concrete or resin has cured for the time the engineer or maker gives.
Level base plates on packers or levelling nuts, then grout under them if the drawing asks.

head: Method
Advantages
Disadvantages
Example
rows: Heat and distortion; skilled welders and inspection; cannot be taken apart
Gate leaves; the side frames of a stand
Can be taken apart; no hot work on site; parts travel flat
Accurate holes needed; bolts can loosen; holes weaken parts slightly
Bracing joined on site; a bracket fixed to a wall or beam
Quick, no heat; joins coated or hard-to-weld sheet
Weaker for heavy loads; can loosen with vibration; hard to remove
Sheet covers and panels on a frame

blocks.p: Plan every lift from the weight. Steel weighs about **7 850 kg per cubic metre**, which is about **7.85 kg per square metre for each millimetre of thickness**.
**Worked example.** A 6 mm plate, 2.4 m × 1.2 m: area 2.88 m² × 6 × 7.85 ≈ **136 kg**. Section weights (kg per metre) are in the supplier's tables: multiply by the total length.

ul: Do not lift heavy or awkward items by hand. Use a trolley, pallet truck, chain block, gantry or crane, under a plan.
A team lift needs one person giving the signals, a clear route and a planned place to set the load down.
Use only lifting gear (slings, shackles, eyebolts, chain blocks) marked with its **safe working load** and in date for its inspection. Gear with no tag or a damaged tag is taken out of use.
The wider the angle between sling legs, the **greater the pull in each leg**. Keep the angle at the hook small (the sling's tag gives its limits).
Keep hands clear of **pinch points**; never stand or reach under a suspended load. Use tag lines to steady it.
To work under a raised frame, **support it securely on rated stands or trestles**, never on a pile of offcuts, a jack alone or someone's hands.

blocks.note: Grinding tacks and welds on an assembly: keep the guard on, use a disc rated for the grinder's speed and not cracked, hold the grinder with both hands, and wear safety glasses, a face shield and ear protection. A burst disc can cause serious injury.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Before leaving, check the opening sizes, the drawing, and the gate, hinges, fixings and tools
Mark the post positions from the opening; check the ground or wall
Set posts plumb on two faces, at the right spacing and height; brace them and let the concrete cure for the time given
Fit the hinges with their pins exactly in line, one above the other
Hang the gate on packers to give the right ground clearance and even gaps
Check level, plumb, swing, latch and lock; tighten all fixings
Touch up damaged paint or galvanising, show the customer how it works and record the checks

blocks.note: If the hinge pins are not in a vertical line, the gate will swing open or shut on its own. Check them with a level or plumb line before the fixings are final.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Hot-dip galvanising** (dipping in molten zinc at about 450 °C) protects gates, grilles and stands from rust in salty sea air.

Hollow sections to be galvanised need **vent and drain holes**, placed as the galvaniser advises. Air or water trapped inside can burst a closed member in the hot zinc, and the zinc must be able to flow in and drain out.
Damaged galvanising is touched up with zinc-rich paint; bare steel is primed promptly, as rust starts within hours in humid air.

sections.title: Inspection, records, handover and leading the team

head: Point in the plan
What it means
rows: Work **stops** until the check is made and signed off
The inspector is told and may come to watch; work can go on if they do not attend

blocks.p: Typical hold points on an assembly: parts checked against the list; fit-up of each sub-assembly before welding; after welding and release; final assembly, including base-plate hole positions; before coating; before dispatch.

ul: Write the **actual measurement**, not just a tick. Figures show how close the item is to its limits, show trends (such as a jig starting to drift) and prove later what was delivered.
Record who checked, when, and with which instrument.
A frame that passes its size checks still needs **visual checks**: weld size and quality, every fixing present, tight and marked, sharp edges removed, spatter cleaned, coating sound.

head: Method
Finds
rows: Surface faults, size and shape; always done first
Cracks at or just below the surface of steel
Faults inside the weld, shown on a film or screen

flow: Re-measure to be sure the reading is right
Mark the item and stop it moving on
Raise a **non-conformance report (NCR)**: what is wrong, by how much, and where
Find the cause: parts, setting out, weld order, early release
Decide the action with the supervisor: rework, repair, scrap, or accept as it is
To accept it as it is, get the customer's or engineer's **written** approval (a concession)
Re-check after any correction, record the result and close the NCR; change the method so it does not happen again

blocks.note: Never send out an item that is outside tolerance on a spoken "it should be fine", and never change a drawing to match the work. Only the person responsible for the design can approve a change, in writing.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Document
Why it matters
rows: Shows the item meets the drawing
Shows every bolt was tightened to the figure
Shows what was accepted and by whom
Helps with repairs and future orders
Helps the customer keep it safe (for example, check bolts, touch up paint)
Delivery note signed by the customer
Shows it arrived complete and in good order

ul: **Brief** before work: what is being built, the order, the hazards and controls, the quality checks, and who does what.
Give each person a clear role they are trained for: setting out, fitting, tacking and welding, inspecting, signalling lifts.
Check PPE, tools, clamps and lifting gear before work starts.
Supervise at the hold points; stop unsafe work or poor work at once and explain why.
**Coach** rather than take over: watch the person, find the cause of the fault, show the right way, let them practise, then check.
At the end: final check, clean-up, tools away, records complete, and near misses reported.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read an assembly drawing, its parts list, title block, revision and notes.
I can split an item into sub-assemblies and plan an order of work that leaves every joint reachable.
I can set hold points and write an assembly plan with roles, lifts and checks.
I can name common steel sections and parts such as base plates, gussets and cleats.
I can use datums and tolerances, and work out totals, clearances, worst-case errors and diagonals.
I can read weld symbols, including arrow side, other side, site welds, all-round and intermittent welds.
I can check a tape, set out full size, and check square, flatness, twist, level and plumb.
I can explain how heat changes steel sizes and allow for it.
I can build, prove and maintain a simple jig.
I can carry out a fit-up check and put right a wide gap, a mismatch or a frame out of square.
I can explain why welded assemblies distort and choose ways to control it.
I can choose bolts, nuts, washers and holes, tighten them in order to a torque, and record it.
I can choose and set blind rivets and set anchors in concrete.
I can estimate the weight of an assembly and plan a safe lift.
I can install a gate plumb and level so that it swings correctly.
I can record actual measurements, raise an NCR and put together a handover pack.
I can brief, supervise and coach a team at work.

terms: A plate on the bottom of a column or leg, with holes for holding-down bolts
The parts list: every part's mark, size, material and quantity
A slight upward curve built into a beam so it is straight when loaded
Written approval to accept an item that does not fully meet the drawing
The point, line or edge from which measurements are taken
Measuring corner to corner both ways to check that a frame is square
Parts pulled out of shape by weld shrinkage
Parts positioned and tacked ready for welding; also the check made before welding
Coating steel with zinc by dipping it in molten zinc
The total material thickness a blind rivet is made to join
A triangular stiffening plate in a corner
A stage where work stops until a check is made and signed
A frame with stops and clamps that holds parts in the same place every time
Marking joints after a trial assembly so each part goes back in the same place
A step between two edges that should be level
Non-conformance report: the record raised when work does not meet the drawing or specification
Non-destructive testing: testing without damaging the part
Setting a part slightly out of line so shrinkage pulls it true
The strength grade marked on a bolt, such as 8.8
A part moving out of line when released from clamps
A stiff bar fixed across a joint to hold plate edges level
A part of the item built and checked on its own before final assembly
A liquid that sets on bolt threads and stops nuts working loose
How far a size may vary from the size on the drawing
Turning force, measured in newton metres (N m)
A frame not lying flat: one corner lifts
A stage the inspector may watch; work can go on if they do not attend

c1.title: Display-rack frames for a supermarket in Porus
c1.text: Kerry-Ann leads a team at a shop in Porus, Manchester, making 24 identical display-rack frames, 1 500 mm × 900 mm in 25 mm square hollow section, for a supermarket. She builds a jig on the setting-out table with angle stops and toggle clamps; some stops are fixed inside the frame outline. The first frame, measured after welding and release, is 2 mm under size in both length and width. The team records both diagonals of every frame.

c2.title: A generator platform near Guys Hill
c2.text: A shop in Linstead is making a galvanised steel platform for a standby generator at a radio mast near Guys Hill, St Catherine, high on a narrow hill road. It travels in four sub-assemblies, to be bolted together on site with M16 bolts of property class 8.8, matching nuts and washers. Damian, the Level 3 fabricator in charge, must plan the bolting and the trip. The nearest hardware store is an hour's drive from the site.

c3.title: Church hall trusses in Buff Bay
c3.text: Sheldon is setting out roof trusses for a church hall in Buff Bay, Portland. Each truss has a span of 6 000 mm and a rise of 1 250 mm at the centre, and is made from 50 × 50 × 3 square hollow section. After welding, the trusses will be hot-dip galvanised. He sets out the first truss on the yard floor at 7 a.m., when the steel is at about 24 °C; the inspector plans to check it after lunch.

c4.title: A conveyor frame in Bamboo
c4.text: At a shop in Bamboo, St Ann, Tishana's team builds a 4 m × 1.2 m conveyor frame from channel for a bottling plant. The fit-up check was skipped to save time. One long side was fully welded before the other was started, and the clamps were taken off while the frame was still hot. At final inspection the diagonals read 4 180 mm and 4 173 mm; the drawing allows a difference of no more than 4 mm.

c5.title: Lifting a footbridge section in Hope Bay
c5.text: A shop in Hope Bay, Portland, must lift a footbridge section onto trestles for painting. It has a deck of 6 mm steel plate, 6 m × 1.2 m, on a frame of hollow sections that weighs about 180 kg. The shop has a mobile gantry with a 1-tonne chain block and two chain slings. One sling's tag, which shows its safe working load and inspection date, has been torn off.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do before the team makes the other 23 frames?
o: Carry on, since 2 mm is small on a frame of this size
Weld the rest more slowly so they shrink less as they cool
Set the stops out to allow for shrinkage, then prove the jig again
Add a strip of weld along each side of the first frame to lengthen it
questions.why: Welds shrink as they cool, so a jig set exactly to drawing size gives small frames. Setting the stops out by the shrinkage found, then making and measuring another first-off, proves the jig before the batch.

questions.q: Why are the frames hard to lift out of the jig at the stops fixed inside the outline?
o: The frames grow as they cool and press out against the clamps
Spatter has welded the frames to the stops inside them
The toggle clamps lock shut when they get hot from the welding
The frames shrink as they cool and grip the stops inside them
questions.why: A welded frame shrinks inwards as it cools, so stops inside its outline get gripped tight. Stops on the outside, or removable pins inside, let each frame come out freely.

questions.q: By the tenth frame, the recorded difference between the diagonals has crept from 1 mm to 4 mm. What is the most likely cause?
o: A stop or clamp in the jig has moved or worked loose
The steel tape has stretched from being used so often
The later frames were welded on a cooler part of the day
The square hollow section has become harder to weld
questions.why: A steady drift in the records points to the jig. Stops get knocked and clamps loosen with use, which is why a jig is checked at set intervals and the actual readings, not ticks, are recorded.

questions.q: What does "8.8" on the head of the M16 bolts tell Damian about their strength?
o: It can safely carry 8.8 tonnes hanging from it in tension
Tensile strength about 880 MPa, and yield about 800 MPa
Tensile strength at least 800 MPa; yield about 640 MPa
Its yield strength is 88 % of its tensile strength
questions.why: The first number × 100 is the minimum tensile strength in MPa (800); the second × 10 is the yield as a percentage of it (80 %, so about 640 MPa). Grade 8.8 bolts need class 8 nuts.

questions.q: In what order should the bolts in each six-bolt splice be tightened?
o: Snug them all, then tighten criss-cross from the centre out
Fully tighten one end bolt, then work along to the other end
Tighten the two outside bolts fully first, then those in between
Tighten each bolt fully as it is fitted, so none are forgotten
questions.why: Snugging all the bolts first pulls the plates into contact; tightening criss-cross from the centre outwards then squeezes the joint evenly, so no gaps are trapped. Final tightening is to the specified torque, with a paint mark on each.

questions.q: On site, two holes in a brace are 3 mm out of line with the cleat. A fitter reaches for the cutting torch to open them up. What should Damian do?
o: Let him burn them out, then paint over the cut edges
Drive a steel drift through to force the holes into line
Weld the brace to the cleat instead of bolting it there
Stop him, find out why, and get approval before reaming
questions.why: Flame-cut or forced holes damage the steel and the galvanising and weaken the joint. Find the cause (wrong part, wrong position, a bent member), and only ream or re-drill to a size the engineer or supervisor approves.

questions.q: Why should Damian trial-assemble and match-mark the platform in the shop before the trip?
o: So the galvaniser can see which faces need a thicker coat
So the bolts can be left out and bought near the site instead
So the platform can travel in one piece instead of four
So each part fits first time and goes back in its place
questions.why: On a remote hill site there is no workshop and no quick supply of parts. Bolting it up in the shop proves the fit and the fixings, and match-marks let the crew put each part back where it fitted.

questions.q: What is the centre-line length of each rafter, from a corner to the centre of the truss?
questions.why: The rafter is the long side of a right-angled triangle with sides 3 000 mm (half the span) and 1 250 mm (the rise): √(3 000² + 1 250²) = √10 562 500 = 3 250 mm.

questions.q: Because the trusses are made of hollow section, what must be done before they go for galvanising?
o: Vent and drain holes are made where the galvaniser advises
Every hollow member must be filled with water to stop zinc getting in
All the welds must be ground flush so the zinc sticks to them
The ends of every member must be sealed airtight with a plate
questions.why: In zinc at about 450 °C, trapped air or water turns to steam and can burst a sealed member violently. Vent and drain holes let gas out and let zinc flow in and drain away.

questions.q: By early afternoon the bottom chord's steel has warmed from 24 °C to about 49 °C. Taking steel growth as 0.012 mm per metre per °C, about how much longer is the 6 m chord?
o: About 0.3 mm
About 1.8 mm
About 3.6 mm
About 18 mm
questions.why: Growth = 6 m × 0.012 × 25 °C = 1.8 mm. That can matter on a close tolerance, so the inspector should know the time and temperature of each reading, or measure in the cool.

questions.q: What does the final diagonal check show?
o: It passes, with 3 mm to spare
It fails, being 7 mm over the limit
It passes, as both diagonals are over 4 m
It fails, being 3 mm over the limit
questions.why: The difference between the diagonals is 4 180 − 4 173 = 7 mm. The limit is 4 mm, so the frame is 3 mm outside tolerance.

questions.q: From the facts in the case, which two things most likely pulled the frame out of square?
o: One side was welded fully first, and the clamps came off while hot
The channel was too stiff, and the diagonals were measured wrongly
Too many tacks were used, and the welds were too small for the job
The frame was welded in the shop instead of on the bottling plant site
questions.why: Welding one side fully first lets its shrinkage pull the frame before the other side balances it, and hot steel is still shrinking when released. Balanced welding and leaving it held until cool prevent both.

questions.q: The plant's engineer agrees in writing to accept the frame as it is, because its feet have slotted holes. How should Tishana record this?
o: Change the drawing to match the frame, and sign it herself
Write "OK" on the inspection sheet and send the frame out
Raise an NCR and keep the signed concession with it
Measure again until the diagonals come within 4 mm
questions.why: The fault is recorded on a non-conformance report with the actual readings, and the engineer's written concession is kept with it and in the handover pack. Only the designer may change a drawing.

questions.q: Steel plate weighs about 7.85 kg per square metre for each millimetre of thickness. About how much does the deck plate alone weigh?
o: About 57 kg
About 135 kg
About 340 kg
About 2 000 kg
questions.why: Area = 6 × 1.2 = 7.2 m². Weight ≈ 7.2 × 6 × 7.85 ≈ 339 kg. With the 180 kg frame, the section weighs about 520 kg, within the 1-tonne chain block.

questions.q: Why should the two sling legs be set so the angle between them at the hook stays small?
o: A small angle stops the load tilting or swinging as it is lifted
Wide angles make the chain block lift far more slowly and jerkily
Narrow angles let the chain block lift a heavier load than marked
The wider the angle, the greater the pull in each sling leg
questions.why: As the legs spread, each leg must pull harder to hold the same load, until it can exceed its safe working load. Keep within the angles on the sling's tag, and use a spreader beam for wide loads.

questions.q: What should be done with the sling whose tag has been torn off?
o: Use it, as long as it is used with the tagged one
Use it only for loads under half the other sling's rating
Take it out of use until it is inspected and re-tagged
Write its rating on the chain in paint and carry on
questions.why: Without its tag nobody can confirm the sling's safe working load or that it has passed its inspection. It is quarantined until a competent person inspects and re-tags it; use other tagged gear meanwhile.

questions.q: An AWS weld symbol has its fillet triangle drawn above the reference line, with nothing below. Where is the weld made?
o: On the side of the joint the arrow touches
On the side opposite the arrow
On both sides of the joint, as a pair of fillets
On site, after the item has been delivered
questions.why: In the AWS system a symbol below the line means the arrow side, above the line means the other side, and on both sides means both. A site weld is shown by a flag.

questions.q: A newly hung driveway gate in Mandeville keeps swinging shut on its own. What is the most likely fault?
o: The latch is fitted too high on the gate
The ground clearance under the gate is too big
The hinge pins are not in a vertical line
The gate is painted with too heavy a coat
questions.why: If one hinge pin sits out from the line of the other, the gate hangs on a slope and swings towards its lowest point. Set the pins plumb, one above the other, with a level or plumb line.

questions.q: The quality schedule for a handrail job marks the paint check as a witness point. What does that allow?
o: Painting may go on if the inspector, once told, does not come
Painting must stop until the inspector has signed the check off
The painter checks his own work and need not write anything down
The check is made only if the customer asks for it at handover
questions.why: At a hold point work must stop until the check is made and signed. At a witness point the inspector is told and may watch, but work can continue if they do not attend.

questions.q: A trainee wants to rivet the slightly loose hook of his steel tape tight. What should you tell him?
o: Do it, as a loose hook always gives readings that are short
Leave it: it slides by its own thickness, by design
Do it, but check the tape against a known length afterwards
Leave it, as the hook is only there to protect the end of the tape
questions.why: The hook moves by exactly its own thickness, out for a hooked reading and in for a pushed one, so both read true. A bent or worn hook is different: check the tape against a known length before a big job.
